summary: Describes a revised Microsoft Word template for writing Internet Drafts and RFCs. It replaces the earlier template of RFC 3285, works better with Word's outline modes, and aims to be easier to use. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5385 describes a Microsoft Word template that lets an author write an RFC as an ordinary document and still get the plain text file the RFC Editor expects. The template sets up the heading levels, page layout and boilerplate, and a small script cleans up the printed output so that it matches the file exactly.

questions: how to write an internet draft in word
how to turn a word document into an rfc text file
subtitle: A Microsoft Word template and post-processing script for writing Internet Drafts and RFCs with what-you-see-is-what-you-get editing.

tldr.problem: Internet Drafts and RFCs are written in text formatting systems such as nroff, or in XML, and neither gives the author a normal word processor view while writing.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a Word template that redefines the built-in heading and body styles so that Word's outline mode, cross-references and page layout produce the required ASCII, plus a Perl post-processor that turns the printed output into a compliant text file.
tldr.outcome: The printed page and the text file are line-for-line and page-for-page identical, so an author can see exactly what the file will look like. This version replaces RFC 3285 and adds outline-mode support, name-based references and updated boilerplate.

today: RFC 5385 is an Informational document published in February 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an independent submission that replaces the template described in RFC 3285, and the memo says the most recent version of the template and the post-processing scripts are available from the author's website.

sections.title: Why a Word Template for RFCs
sections.content:
Internet Drafts and RFCs are predominantly written in embedded-text, compile-based formatting systems. The primary and first such system is NROFF, a text-formatting utility based on manual entry of embedded configuration commands, such as .p for new paragraphs. XML is a more recent alternative that uses structure tags instead of explicit formatting commands, so that a single file can be compiled into ASCII output, HTML, or a variety of other formats as desired.

Although XML adds more modern semantic information to the structure tags, neither system supports modern WYSIWYG editing. Editors such as Microsoft Word and Corel WordPerfect provide not only WYSIWYG editing but also semantic tags and outline-mode capabilities. A Word template called 2-Word.template.rtf was created to support authoring RFCs, as described in RFC 3285. That version succeeded in enabling Word-based RFC editing, but did not support Word's outline mode renumbering capabilities.

This document describes a revised Word template file, 2-Word-v2.0.template.dot, intended as an update to that of RFC 3285. It redefines basic styles such as Normal and Heading1 rather than creating new styles, updates the boilerplate according to BCP 78, uses more conventional methods for autonumbered references and figures including support for name-based references such as [Tou2005], and supports direct output to a printer from the .doc source as well as the RFC 3285 style print to text with post-processing on Windows-based PCs. The document assumes familiarity with Microsoft Windows operating systems and the Word application.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing an RFC in a text markup language means writing commands instead of formatting. The template lets the author type in Word as usual, and turns that into the plain text the RFC Editor wants.

sections.title: Using the Template
sections.content:
To use the template, double-click on it in Windows; it may work in MacOS or OpenOffice, but this has not been confirmed. The result should be a new document. The document should not be opened from within Word, for example through the File and Open menu, because that edits the template rather than using it to create a new template-based document.

The template provides a number of styles. Some are redefined internal styles, such as Normal, Heading1-9, Caption, Header and Footer, which are used in the normal fashion with tabs as desired. New styles include RFC Title for the document title only, RFC Figure for ASCII-art figures, which are single spaced and kept together, RFC List Bullet and RFC List Numbered for lists, RFC References for normative and informative references, and RFC App and RFC App H1-5 for appendix titles and headings in A. format.

Throughout the document the author should avoid bold, italics, any other character formatting, and any graphics or paragraph or table borders. Smart hyphens and quotes need not be avoided, because the post-processor translates them into RFC-compatible ASCII. The current styles allow existing hyphens to break across lines but do not add hyphenation; to insert a non-breaking hyphen, type the control-underscore sequence, which is particularly useful in URLs. It is critical not to use any styles other than those provided by the template.

When saving, the template is provided as a Word 97-2003 .dot template, and Word 2007 uses an XML-based .dotx variant. Word 2007 can use .dot templates in Compatibility Mode, in which case the saved file has a .doc suffix, while a file saved in native Word 2007 mode has .docx format. It does not matter which saved file format is used.
sections.plainLanguage: Double-click the template, then use only the styles it gives you. The template has already set the margins, the page breaks, the heading numbering and the boilerplate, so anything you do by hand risks breaking the layout.

sections.title: Getting the ASCII Output
sections.content:
The template supports printing similar output both to regular printers on 8.5 by 11 inch paper and as Internet-Draft and RFC compatible text files. Printing to a printer is designed for Windows XP and Vista and may work with earlier versions of Windows; it has not been tested with other operating systems. Printing to text is supported only for Windows at this time, and there is no current support for XML.

The output to a printer is line-for-line and page-for-page identical with the text-only version, with minor exceptions: single and double quotes may be angled rather than straight, depending on whether smart quotes are enabled in the AutoCorrect options, and hyphens may print as an em dash or en dash depending on whether smart hyphens are enabled.

Producing a text file is a two-step process on Windows XP or Vista. First a .prn file is generated by printing the document to a text-only printer, the Generic and Text Only printer found under Generic in the print drivers list, configured to save to a file. Second, the printed file is run through the post-processor, which is given as an appendix. The post-processor omits carriage returns, converting CR LF to LF and omitting bare CRs, converts smart quotes and hyphens to their ASCII counterparts, omits the blank lines between the footer of one page and the header of the next and inserts a form-feed between the two, and checks for remaining illegal characters, that is anything that is not printable ASCII, CR or LF.
sections.plainLanguage: To get the text file, print the document to a printer called Generic, Text Only and save the result as a file, then run the script over that file. The script removes the carriage returns, turns smart quotes back into plain ones, and marks the page breaks.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 3285
sections.content:
The document and the template borrow heavily from RFC 3285, and all specifics of point sizes, tab locations and the automatic date fields come directly from that template. Four things changed. Heading styles are handled by redefining Normal, Heading1-9, Header, Footer and Caption, rather than by defining new RFC-named styles as in RFC 3285, because the use of internal style names is required for proper operation of outline mode, notably when promoting or demoting sections and renumbering the headings within them. This is common practice in Microsoft-supplied templates and in those of the IEEE and ACM.

The reference style is the second change, and there are two of them. RFC References cross-references using numbers such as [1] and is a body text paragraph style that autonumbers on the [1] format, which differs from RFC 3285, where references were inserted as endnotes. Putting references in endnotes has unexpected behaviour: a reference is defined by its first use as a citation, so removing the first citation removes the reference entirely despite other cross-references, which does not happen with autonumbered body text paragraphs. RFC References Bookmark uses Word's bookmarking cross-reference features to support name and year cross-references such as [Tou2005], and is expected to be the preferred format for future Internet Drafts and RFCs. Authors format these references manually with a suggested tag of the first three letters of the first author and the year of the document, for example [Bra2004], with a trailing lowercase letter to separate two references that would otherwise collide, such as [Bra2004a] and [Bra2004b].

The third change is that the boilerplate was updated to conform with current RFC Editor requirements, notably the BCP 78 rights statements, and it is written in regular text so that authors can keep it up to date. The fourth is simplification: headers and footers use conventional tabbing rather than tables, users no longer need to avoid smart quotes or hyphens, and a number of styles keep headings with the text that follows them and keep list items, references and figure lines together, so that nothing is split awkwardly across a page boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: The main change is that the template now uses Word's own heading styles instead of new ones with special names, which is what makes the outline mode work. References can be numbered the old way or cited by name, and the boilerplate is plain text that an author can update.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo notes that there are many security issues in the general use of Microsoft operating systems and applications, and that this template is not known to expose any new security issues: it contains no macros as developed and deployed. The author considered including the MD5 signatures of the current versions of the .dot template and the Perl post-processor files. The current post-processor file is included in the document as an appendix, while the .dot file is updated to track the current requirements of the IETF boilerplate, so its MD5 signature cannot be included there, but is posted on the author's website for verification.
sections.plainLanguage: The template holds no macros, so it does not add any risk of its own. The author publishes a checksum of the current files so that a user can check they have the right ones.

viz.caption: WHAT THE POST-PROCESSOR DOES TO THE PRINTED FILE

data.title: Post-processing steps
data.code:
Omits <CR>s (converts <CR><LF> to <LF> and omits bare <CR>s).
Converts smart quotes and hyphens to their ASCII counterparts.
Omits blank lines between the footer of one page and the header of
the next, and inserts a <CTL-L> (form-feed) between the two.
Checks for remaining illegal characters (not printable ASCII, CR, LF).
